guide.title: Redundancy is an availability feature. Backup is a recovery feature. They fail in different directions and neither substitutes for the other.
guide.summary: A RAIDZ pool survives losing one, two or three drives depending on its parity level, and that is genuinely valuable — a failed disk becomes a scheduled errand instead of an outage. But every threat that reaches the filesystem reaches every copy in the array at once: an accidental delete, an encrypting worm, a bad cable corrupting writes, a house fire. The list of things RAID does not cover is longer than the list it does.
points: RAIDZ1/2/3 tolerate one, two and three simultaneous drive failures. The number is parity, not safety.
Resilver reads every remaining disk end to end, which is the heaviest and longest sustained load the array ever sees — and it happens while redundancy is already reduced.
ZFS detects silent corruption because it checksums data and metadata; traditional RAID only knows a drive is gone, not that it returned the wrong bytes.
Snapshots protect against mistakes, not against losing the pool. They live on the same disks as the data.
3-2-1 is the rule the other four points imply: three copies, two media, one off-site.
